lie.title: Not a Word of a Lie
opening: The donkey bit him at ten past five.

Davie McGarrity had been church officer at St Fillan’s Parish Church for twenty-two years, and in that time he had been bitten by a Session clerk’s Jack Russell, a toddler at a christening and, memorably, a retired Moderator of the General Assembly who had been sleepwalking in the manse. He had never been bitten by a donkey. It was, he decided, holding his forearm in the falling snow, the most personal of the lot.

“She doesnae mean it,” said the girl from the petting farm. She was about nineteen and had the look of someone who had driven a horsebox over the moor in a blizzard and would not be doing it again. “Clementine’s just nervous round men.”
“I’m nervous round her,” said Davie. “We’ve that in common.”
Clementine regarded him with the flat, ancient contempt of an animal that knew exactly what it was doing. Then she ate a length of tinsel off the stable roof.
lines: I tried to lie to a man selling double glazing once and I ended up buying a conservatory.
He did the crossword in the Daily Record in biro, because pencil was for people who expected to be wrong.
It turned out that people would come a long way, in the West of Scotland, to listen to a man who could not lie to them, even if most of what he said was about his knee.

cable.title: The Cable and the Quiet
lines: Ewan disliked the word temporarily when nobody could identify the conditions under which the temporary state would end.
Ewan's flat had always been quiet, but that was not the same thing.
His father stood in the doorway with the hall light behind him, smaller in it than Ewan usually let himself notice.

veilborn.title: Echoes of the Shattered
opening: The Archive received the dead.

Not their bodies, Lyrinth had other institutions for bodies, and the dead themselves, in the Archive's taxonomy, were not the point. What the Archive received were their moments: the crystallised instants of experience that certain Glassborn could fix and hold, the way amber fixed insects, the way ice fixed the shape of a footprint until the thaw. Moment-echoes. The dead left them scattered through the fabric of where they had lived, snagged on doorframes and window-glass and the surfaces of still water, and the Archive's work was to collect them, catalogue them, and make them available to those who needed to find something in the past.

It was an honest work. Tselin had decided this early and had not reconsidered. The alternative, that she had spent seventeen years in a building full of other people's moments because she was afraid of her own, she had considered and set aside. Repeatedly. With the focused deliberateness of someone who knew exactly what they were setting aside.
lines: A Grannakh hillside, read correctly, was a biography.
Vaelra had been eating grief for forty-one years.
She was beginning to understand that the line had always been a choice, not a fact.

veilborn2.title: Cradle's Veil
opening: The echo arrived on a Tuesday, in a crate of eleven, from a recovery site that should not have produced it.

Tselin had been at the long table since seven. The north-facing windows were bright and cold behind her, and the collection-cloth in front of her held the morning's work: domestic echoes from a merchant's house on the Shardwater, three of them dull and four of them lovely, a cook's afternoon and a child's birthday and a man reading a letter twice. She had logged them. Origin, date-estimate, recovery location, condition. She had set them aside.

She had opened seven thousand and sixty-one moment-echoes in seventeen years and four months. She noted the number the way she always noted it, without pride, as a fact about the work. What she noted now, and had been noting for six weeks, was that the number no longer felt like a wall built one brick at a time. It felt like what it was: seven thousand and sixty-one people who had stood somewhere and felt something and left it behind without meaning to.
lines: It was warm the way a hand was warm when someone had just let go of it.
"There's an inside," Tselin said. "I didn't know there was an inside."
Nine threads, fraying. One knot, pulled.

veilborn3.title: When Realms Become One
opening: At dusk the crystal bridge showed Grannakh.

It had not always. For the first weeks after the Veil it had shown only what it had always shown, which was Lyrinth: the towers in their impossible geometries, the light coming off every face of them and splitting and going on, so that a person crossing at evening walked through a hundred small rainbows and did not look at any of them, because they had seen them every evening of their lives. Then, in the eighth week, the light had begun to go somewhere else.
Tselin stood at the eastern rail, where she stood every evening now, and watched it go.
lines: Tselin's hands were glass to the elbow.
Korr's letters were the shape of what he was able to say, and what he was able to say had got larger in the Cradle, and it would take a while to get larger still.
The grey of no people.

clarity.title: Clarity
opening: The road narrowed before the loch appeared, bending through trees that pressed close enough to the verge to make the morning feel darker than it was. Strachan drove with the window cracked despite the cold, a cigarette burning between two fingers of his left hand, the smoke pulled outside whenever the car gathered speed and curling back towards him whenever he slowed. The car was a nine year old Vauxhall with a heater that worked on one setting, which was off. Malik had stopped commenting on the smoke ten minutes earlier. She had not stopped commenting on the heater.
"I can feel my knees," she said.
"That's what they're for."
"I mean I can feel them as separate objects."

She sat angled towards the passenger window with her notebook closed on her lap and a paper cup of coffee from a petrol station in Balloch, held in both hands like a hot water bottle. Through the trunks, in glimpses, the water came and went. She watched it a little longer each time than the job required. Strachan noticed and said nothing. He had worked beside her for six years and understood that a lake was one of the few things Malik did not discuss.
lines: A tick was a very small thing to carry that much.
The city did not hold things in place. It took them in, worked round them, buried them under movement, and kept going.
"They saw it. They recorded it. That isn't the same thing."

underpainting.title: Underpainting
opening: The house in Milngavie had the silence of a place that had been lived in by one person for eleven years and was now, finally, being lived in by nobody at all, and Elaine Sorley had learned, three weekends into clearing it, that this silence had its own weight, different from the ordinary quiet of an empty room.

She worked through the study first, on the theory that paperwork would be worse the longer she left it, and found her father's filing exactly as she'd have predicted, meticulous in the way of a man who had spent forty years as a quantity surveyor and had never once, in her memory, lost a receipt. Bank statements in date order. Insurance documents in a labelled folder. A will she'd already seen, at the solicitor's, three weeks ago, that had left her the house and its contents with the same brisk clarity he'd have brought to costing a roof.

The painting was the last thing she had been putting off. It hung on the half-landing, where it had hung for as long as Elaine had been alive, a woman in grey she had said good morning to on the way down to breakfast every day of her childhood, and she had walked past it for three weekends without looking at it properly. On the Sunday she finally lifted it off its hook, surprised by the weight, and carried it to the window to see it in the daylight, a woman looking out from a canvas gone dark with age, dressed in something that might have been Victorian or might simply have been old-fashioned even when it was painted, her expression neither warm nor unwelcoming, just watchful. Behind her on the wallpaper the hook left a pale rectangle, cleaner than the wall around it, the shape of forty years.
lines: Behind her on the wallpaper the hook left a pale rectangle, cleaner than the wall around it, the shape of forty years.
"You do love an orphaned object, don't you. Something nobody else has bothered to properly ask about."
"I think some things get buried because somebody decided, once, carefully, that burying them was the kinder choice."

A Christmas comedy of crime, love and one very offended spirit. It’s Christmas Eve in Carrickmuir, the snow has shut the town in, and there’s a real baby in the nativity manger with a note: keep him safe, not the polis. Senga Rennie wants the baby. And something buried under the kirk since 1647 has woken up, and it climbs inside anyone who tells a lie.

In the west of Scotland, on Christmas Eve, that is nearly everybody.

posts.label: Beadle, noun
posts.headline: The one who has the keys.
posts.sub: In a Scottish kirk, the beadle is the church officer: the one who unlocks the doors, carries in the Bible before the minister and knows where everything is kept. Davie McGarrity has been beadle at St Fillan’s for twenty-two years. Before that, he opened safes.
posts.caption:
Every kirk had one. Some still do.

Not a Word of a Lie is about one beadle, one Christmas Eve, and the night his old skills come in very handy.

What’s the most Scottish job title you know?

Not a Word of a Lie. Out now.

posts.label: Christmas Eve
posts.caption:
It’s Christmas Eve.

In Carrickmuir, the snow is coming down, the donkey has already bitten the beadle, and something very old is waking up under the kirk. It moves into anyone who tells a lie.

So tonight, be honest. Merry Christmas from Carrickmuir.

Not a Word of a Lie. Out now in Kindle, paperback and hardback.

posts.label: Provenance, noun
posts.headline: Where a thing has been.
posts.sub: In the art world, provenance is the documented history of a work: who made it, who owned it, and how it passed from hand to hand. A gap in that history can be innocent. It can also be where the trouble starts.
posts.caption:
Why it’s called The Provenance Series.

Dr Alec Muir authenticates paintings. He knows every object has a history, and that the gaps in it are where people hide things.

If you could know the full history of one object you own, which would it be?

Pentimento, book one. Out now in Kindle, paperback and hardback.

Kindle, paperback and hardback.

Debunked is out now.

Callum Ferris makes his living on a Glasgow podcast, taking apart claims of the paranormal. Then his grandmother, on her deathbed, says something she had no way of knowing.

A psychological thriller with real science in it, and a narrator who copes with almost anything by making a joke of it.

The Noisy Mind is out now, in paperback and Kindle.

For anyone whose mind replays the conversation, rereads the text, and keeps checking long after everyone else has moved on.

The Cable and the Quiet.

Ewan McLeod keeps a GP practice running: the phones, the complaints, the rota, and the store cupboard where a spare network cable sits coiled on the lower shelf. On Thursdays he visits his father, in a house that has been quieter since his mother died. Everyone depends on Ewan. Nobody asks who he depends on.

A novel about grief, about work, and about the people on both sides of the desk. Expected release: Autumn 2027.

slides.text: Almost everyone who lives with anxiety arrives at the same question. It tends to come late, after the thing has happened again, when the worst of it has passed and only the tiredness is left.
If I know my fear isn't rational, why does it still feel so real?
You can know it. The person in the middle of a panic attack often knows, even then, that a racing heart is not a heart attack.
The body answers as though the danger were already in the room. The knowing and the feeling come apart, and you are left somewhere between the two.
Here is the part that changes things. Your brain does not wait for the world and then react to it. It runs slightly ahead, predicting what is about to happen and readying you for it.

posts.caption:
The question almost everyone with anxiety ends up asking, and where the answer starts.

Swipe through the opening of The Calibrated Mind. Out now.

slides.text: The scaffolding on Fotheringay Road had been up for six weeks, and Mara Kerr had learned to read it the way other people read weather. This morning it told her nothing had moved since Friday.

Category B listed, 1887, a tenement that had survived two world wars and a botched harling job in the seventies and was now, apparently, going to be undone by a leaking gutter nobody had looked at since devolution.

She liked the argument of it. The building told you what was wrong with it if you looked properly, and then you told the owners, and the owners argued, and somewhere in the argument was the truth, usually.

posts.caption:
Swipe for the opening of Pentimento, book one of The Provenance Series.

Mara Kerr reads old Glasgow buildings for what they're hiding. She has somewhere to be at half past, and a Thursday she's keeping to herself.

Expected release: December 2026.

Rewiring Pain is out now.

How the brain learns pain, and how it can learn safety again. A plain guide to modern pain science for anyone who has lived with pain longer than anyone expected.

This book is not about pretending pain isn't real. It's about understanding what your nervous system has been trying to do.

posts.text: He thought of himself as precise, and precision in the upper sky was a form of power that did not require permission.

Threnvald, high above the valley of Edrath, in the first pages of The Roots That Breathe.

Book one of The Dimming Canopy, a five-book epic fantasy about power, restraint, and what a bond costs when it's used without asking. Expected release: June 2027.

slides.text: There is a particular kind of mind that rarely becomes quiet.
If this describes you, you are not alone. And your mind is not broken.

The same systems that produce the noise also produce sensitivity, depth, and insight. These are qualities the world quietly depends on. The difficulty is not that your mind thinks. The difficulty is that it does not know when to stop.

You do not need a quieter mind.
You need a better relationship with the one you have.

posts.caption:
Swipe through the first page of The Noisy Mind.

For the mind that replays the conversation, rereads the message, and keeps checking long after everyone else has moved on.

Out now in paperback and Kindle.

posts.text: "There's your grandfather," she said. "In his good jumper."
posts.caption:
Six words, an hour before the end. The exact jumper he was buried in, twenty-two years earlier.

Callum has a professional explanation for this. Several, in fact. None of them will stick.

The Calibrated Mind. Retraining anxiety, panic, OCD and trauma-related fear using modern brain science.

You are not broken. You are miscalibrated.

Out now.

posts.text: A nervous system that has learned pain can also learn safety.
posts.caption:
Pain is real. It's also a protective output of the brain and nervous system, which is why it can carry on after tissues have healed, and why understanding it can change it.

Rewiring Pain. Out now.

posts.label: Pentimento, noun
posts.headline: What shows through.
posts.sub: A pentimento is the trace of an earlier image beneath a painting's surface, where the artist changed their mind and painted over it. Time and thinning paint let the first version back out. The word comes from the Italian for repenting.
posts.caption:
Why the book is called Pentimento.

Dr Alec Muir authenticates paintings for a living. He is very good at finding what lies beneath. The Provenance Series is about people, families and towns that carry earlier versions of themselves just under the surface.

Which word from art or science do you love the sound of?

posts.text: There was a stretch of time when I cried at the wheel on the way to work, three or four mornings a week, for no reason I could point to. Same drive I'd done for years. Nothing had changed except what was running underneath it, and that had become more than I could carry quietly. I assumed for a long time that this was just what a mind did. It isn't.
posts.caption:
Where The Noisy Mind begins.

If your mind rarely goes quiet, you are not alone in it, and none of it means something is wrong with you.

posts.label: The Calibrated Mind
posts.headline: The smoke alarm isn't broken.
posts.sub: It goes off when the toast browns because it is doing the one thing alarms do. What has moved is the threshold. Anxiety works the same way: the signals are real, and the point where they get read as an emergency has shifted.
posts.caption:
A thermometer that reads a few degrees high isn't broken. Every part of it works. What has drifted is the relationship between what it reads and what is true.

That's calibration, and it's what The Calibrated Mind is about. Out now.

slides.text: If you are reading this, chances are you have lived with pain longer than anyone ever expected, possibly longer than you expected.
You may have tried to be patient. You may have tried to be brave. You may have rested, pushed through, stretched, strengthened, medicated, waited.
Let us start here, clearly and gently: you are not broken. Pain is not a personal failure. It is not weakness. It is not a character flaw.
Pain is a signal, a powerful one. And signals can change.

For anyone who has lived with pain longer than anyone expected, and been told everything looks normal.

slides.text: The lights in reception were already on when Ewan arrived, though the practice itself had not yet begun.

He preferred the building at this hour, not because he disliked the staff, or even the patients, though there were individual examples of both about whom he was prepared to remain undecided, but because it was simply easier to understand the place before it filled.
Near the skirting below it, the grey network cable had worked loose from the plastic trunking again.
It wasn't a repair. It was no longer a trip hazard. For the moment those were close enough to the same thing.

Rewiring Pain. Out now.

posts.label: Behind the book
posts.headline: The strange science is real.
posts.sub: Princeton ran a lab testing whether minds could nudge machines for nearly thirty years. The Global Consciousness Project has watched random number generators around the world since 1998. The US government paid for remote viewing. Debunked invents the people and the danger. Not the research.
posts.caption:
Everything odd that Callum investigates in Debunked has a real history behind it: the Princeton Engineering Anomalies Research lab, the Global Consciousness Project, the remote-viewing programmes, placebo studies and meditation neuroscience.

The question the book asks is simple. What if someone found a way to make money from it?

slides.text: I have watched, in a professional capacity, forty-one people greet on cue for strangers pretending to be their dead husbands. I have a spreadsheet. It has colour-coded tabs.

A pal once asked, not unkindly, whether I needed a hobby that didn't involve quantifying other people's grief, and I told her the spreadsheet was the hobby, which she found less reassuring than I'd intended.
None of the forty-one prepared me for my own grandmother.
An hour before the end she opened her eyes, which by then had been shut so long I'd started addressing my remarks to the general vicinity of her face like a man leaving a voicemail.

posts.caption:
Swipe for how Debunked begins.

Callum Ferris debunks psychics for a living. He has a spreadsheet for everything. Then his grandmother says something on her deathbed that no spreadsheet can explain.

Debunked is out now.

posts.text: You didn't choose to open this investigation. It opened itself, and now some part of you is standing inside it, going through the evidence.
posts.caption:
Someone pauses half a second too long, or a text comes back shorter than usual.

If you know what happens next in your head, this book was written for you. The Noisy Mind. Out now.

posts.text: Anxiety is not a failure of logic. It is what happens when the predictions have been tuned toward danger. And a system that has been tuned can be tuned again.

posts.headline: Pain grows louder in a body that does not feel safe.
posts.sub: A nervous system that feels threatened tightens muscles, sharpens attention and heightens sensation. That isn't imagined. It is physiology, and safety can be learned.
posts.caption:
Why fear and pain feed each other, and why the way out is gradual, patient and possible.

Rewiring Pain. Out now.

slides.text: Threnvald circled where the air thinned into a cold so clean it felt like a blade drawn along the tongue.

The valley of Edrath lay open beneath him, arranged into greens and browns and river-silver, a place that could almost pass for peaceful when he was still high enough to forget what waited beneath it.
He did not think of himself as beautiful, because beauty was a human way of judging things, and humans judged things so they could decide what to claim.
He inhaled deeply and iron entered his mouth.

slides.text: Dovra woke before the birds did, which was the only way to wake at the Farrow Post if she wanted the ground quiet enough to hear anything in it.
Three rotations at Farrow, and the ground had never once surprised her.

A goat, currently regarding her with the flat contempt goats reserved for anyone who had not yet fed them.
Dovra fed the goat.

By evening she had eaten, banked the fire, and settled with her ledger to copy the day's marks into the fair record she would carry back at the end of the rotation, a chore she found close to meditative by now, the neat repetition of it, line after line of the ground saying nothing had changed.
She was two lines into it when the ground said something had changed.

posts.text: Somewhere beneath the waiting, for the first time, the ground had begun to listen back.
posts.caption:
The Telaru don't fight with fire. They listen to the roots.

The Roots That Breathe, book one of The Dimming Canopy. Coming soon.

posts.text: Eleven months later, not one of those words has agreed to stick to my grandfather's jumper. They just sort of slide off it and sit there, looking at me.
posts.caption:
Confabulation. Terminal lucidity. Callum has used these words with real confidence on television.

slides.text: I was recognised, three times last month, in circumstances distinctive enough that I have started, against my own better instincts, cataloguing them the way I once catalogued mediums.

A woman at a petrol station outside Perth, filling her tank at the pump beside mine, who simply said, "You're the biscuit man," with such complete confidence that I did not have the heart to correct either the nickname or its source.

A teenager on the Glasgow Subway who filmed me for eleven seconds without asking, uploaded it with the caption "the guy from the psychic murder podcast," and generated, by his own later, cheerfully unrepentant account, forty thousand views by lunchtime.

posts.caption:
Eighteen months after Debunked, Callum Ferris is a little bit famous, and not enjoying it.

Swipe for three sightings. Inherited, the sequel to Debunked, is coming soon.

slides.text: I have watched, in a professional capacity, forty-one people greet on cue for strangers pretending to be their dead husbands. I have a spreadsheet. It has colour-coded tabs.

A pal once asked, not unkindly, whether I needed a hobby that didn’t involve quantifying other people’s grief, and I told her the spreadsheet was the hobby, which she found less reassuring than I’d intended.
None of the forty-one prepared me for my own grandmother.

posts.text: A pause that meant nothing at the time can grow heavier with every replay.
posts.caption:
It's two in the morning and you're back in the meeting. Not the whole meeting. Just the bit where you said the thing.

The replay feels like thinking. It isn't. Nothing new arrives on the fortieth lap, and the person across the table went home and forgot about it hours ago.

Send this to someone who replays conversations in bed.

The Noisy Mind. Out now.

slides.label: Save this for 2am
slides.headline: Why it gets louder at night
slides.sub: Four passages from The Noisy Mind for anyone whose mind starts reviewing the day the moment the light goes off. Swipe through.

slides.text: Lying down to sleep, your body's ready to rest but your mind starts reviewing the day anyway, replaying conversations, drafting tomorrow, circling small uncertainties, and it can genuinely feel louder than it did that morning.
That's part of why rumination tends to peak late at night: you're tired, but you're also finally undistracted, and thoughts that got pushed aside all day come back with more force than before.

Ask yourself, mid-thought, plainly: am I solving something, or just replaying it? If nothing new is coming out of the thinking, you already have your answer, and naming it quietly, this is rumination, tends to loosen the grip more than arguing with it ever does.

And if your mind is still busy once you're in bed, writing down whatever's unfinished, a worry, a task, an idea, tends to quiet it more than you'd expect, because it reassures your brain that nothing will be lost if it stops holding onto it.

posts.caption:
Four passages from The Noisy Mind for the hour when everything else has gone quiet.

Save it for the next time you're lying awake going over the day. And send it to the friend who messages you at 1am because they can't switch off.

The Noisy Mind. Out now.

posts.text: The brain takes the wrong lesson from that relief. It decides the escape is what kept you safe, and it files both the escape and the original threat as proven.
posts.caption:
Checking the door again. Asking if that message sounded rude. Searching a symptom at midnight. The relief is real, and it's exactly what keeps the fear in place.

Send this to someone who's always checking.

The Calibrated Mind. Out now.

slides.label: Save this
slides.headline: Why reassurance makes anxiety worse
slides.sub: Swipe for why, and for a kinder way to step off the loop.

slides.text: Checking the door again. Asking if that message sounded rude. Searching a symptom at midnight. The relief is real. It just doesn't last.
Every time checking works, your brain learns the wrong thing. Not 'there was no danger', but 'there was danger, and checking saved me'. The fear never gets tested, so it never fades.
Try delay, not a ban. When the urge to check arrives, put it off for ten minutes. Watch the anxiety rise, then start to come down on its own. That curve is the test your brain has been missing.

Recalibration does not come from reassurance. It does not come from arguing with your thoughts, pushing them down, or trying to switch the feeling off. It comes from giving the system something it cannot ignore, which is new information in a form it has to learn from.

posts.caption:
Reassurance brings relief within minutes, and that relief is what keeps the fear in place. Swipe for why, and for a gentler way out.

If checking or reassurance is taking over your days, talk to your GP about talking therapy. And if a symptom is new or changing, get it looked at first.

Send this to someone who's stuck in the loop.

The Calibrated Mind. Out now.

posts.label: Rewiring Pain
posts.headline: The nail went straight through his boot.
posts.sub: The pain was so bad he had to be sedated before it could be pulled out. When they took the boot off, the nail had passed cleanly between his toes. His foot was uninjured. The pain was real. The damage wasn't.
posts.caption:
A case reported in the BMJ in 1995: a builder jumped down onto a 15 cm nail, and the smallest movement of it was agony. His brain saw a nail through his boot and gave him the pain of the worst.

Pain is something the brain produces to protect you, not a measurement of damage. That's why it can carry on after an injury has healed, and why it can change.

Send this to someone who's been told their scan is clear.

Rewiring Pain. Out now.

slides.label: Rewiring Pain
slides.headline: The scan was clear. So why does it still hurt?
slides.sub: Swipe for what's actually going on.

slides.text: They may be told that scans are normal or that nothing alarming has been found, yet the pain they experience is anything but normal. The body still hurts. Movement still feels uncertain. Life begins to organise itself around the need to avoid making things worse.
In persistent pain, tissues may be healed or healing, but the nervous system remains on high alert and the protective response does not switch off.

Think of a smoke alarm that goes off when toast burns. It is not malfunctioning out of malice, it is doing exactly what it was designed to do, just with the volume turned up too high. Persistent pain often works in the same way.
Overprotective pain feels real because it is real. The sensations are genuine. The distress is genuine. The impact on life is genuine.

posts.caption:
Normal scans, healed tissue, and it still hurts. That isn't imagined.

New pain, or pain with other symptoms, needs a proper check first. This is about the pain that has been checked and still won't let go.

Send this to someone who's tired of being told nothing's wrong.

Rewiring Pain. Out now.

posts.label: The Noisy Mind
posts.headline: Nobody else is replaying it.
posts.sub: In a Cornell study, students wore an embarrassing T-shirt into a room of their peers. They guessed half the room had noticed. About a quarter had. The person you're worrying about went home and forgot it.
posts.caption:
We think we're lit up on a stage. Mostly, people are busy with their own lives. The comment you're still going over was, for them, ten seconds of an ordinary Tuesday.

Send this to someone still thinking about something they said last week.

The Noisy Mind. Out now.

posts.text: Persistent pain often reflects an overprotective alarm system rather than ongoing damage.
posts.caption:
The alarm is sensitive, not accurate. A movement that hurts isn't necessarily doing harm, and a nervous system that has learned pain can learn safety.

Send this to someone who's been living with pain longer than anyone expected.

Rewiring Pain. Out now.

posts.text: You've felt this: a message sent in five seconds during a busy afternoon, gone from your mind until it isn't, hours later, replaying itself word by word.
posts.caption:
Then the rereading starts. Was it too blunt? Did that full stop sound annoyed? Why haven't they replied?

Send this to someone who rereads their own texts.

The Noisy Mind. Out now.

posts.text: The model grows surer of a threat the world stopped supplying long ago.
posts.caption:
Why an old fear can feel stronger now than when it started. Every check, every escape, every avoided moment takes away the one experience that would turn it down: finding out that the disaster doesn't come.

Send this to someone whose anxiety has outlived its reason.

The Calibrated Mind. Out now.
